passage_title: Warm Water and Coral Bleaching
passage:
Reef-building corals are animals whose tissues contain single-celled algae called symbionts. The symbionts make sugars by photosynthesis and pass much of this food to the coral. When the surrounding water stays unusually warm for days or weeks, many corals expel their symbionts and turn pale, a response called bleaching.

Researchers collected fragments of three coral species, Species P, Species Q, and Species R, from the same reef. For each species, 20 fragments were held for 14 days in a tank of seawater kept at each of six constant temperatures. At the end of the 14 days, the researchers recorded the percent of fragments still alive and measured the average symbiont density (millions of symbiont cells per square centimeter of coral surface) of the surviving fragments. A species was classified as bleached at a given temperature if its average symbiont density at that temperature was less than half of its average symbiont density at 27 °C. Table 1 shows the results.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Average symbiont density and percent survival of coral fragments after 14 days at each water temperature

prompt: According to Table 1, what was the average symbiont density of Species R fragments held at 30 °C?
explanation: In the 30 °C row, the Species R density column reads 1.9. The value 1.4 is Species Q at 30 °C, 1.5 is Species P at 30 °C, and 2.6 is Species R at 29 °C.
subskill: read a value from a table

passage_title: Craters on the Lava Plains of Orvane
passage:
Meteorites strike the surfaces of rocky planets throughout their history, so craters accumulate over time: the longer a surface has existed, the more craters it has per unit area. Planetary scientists used orbiter images to count craters on five surface units (Units 1 through 5) of lava rock on Orvane, a hypothetical rocky planet. Table 1 gives the number of craters in three size classes, and the total, per 10,000 km² of each unit.

The scientists estimate that the age of a lava surface on Orvane, in billions of years, equals the total number of craters per 10,000 km² divided by 100. On a surface from which no craters have been erased, craters 1 to 2 km across are about twice as numerous as craters 2 to 5 km across. On some units, windblown dust can bury and erase craters smaller than 2 km across; craters 2 km across or larger are too deep to be erased this way.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Number of craters per 10,000 km² on five surface units of Orvane

prompt: According to Table 1, how many craters 2 to 5 km across were counted per 10,000 km² on Unit 4?
explanation: In the Unit 4 row, the 2 to 5 km column reads 35. The value 10 is the count of craters more than 5 km across, 70 is the count of craters 1 to 2 km across, and 115 is the total for Unit 4.

passage_title: LED Light Color and Seedling Growth
passage:
Plants use light for photosynthesis, and the color of the light can also change the way a plant grows. Researchers grew seedlings of Species W, an unnamed leafy herb, in growth chambers lit only by panels of light-emitting diodes (LEDs) for 16 hours per day. Light intensity was measured as photon flux, the amount of light reaching each square meter of leaf surface per second, in micromoles of photons per square meter per second (µmol/m²/s). In every trial, 12 seedlings were grown for 21 days at 22 °C. Each plant's stem length was then measured, and the plant was dried and weighed. Table 1 gives the average dry mass and stem length per plant. Unless stated otherwise, the photon flux was 200 µmol/m²/s.

Experiment 1
Seedlings were grown under red LEDs only, blue LEDs only, green LEDs only, a mixture of red and blue LEDs in which 50% of the photons were blue, or white LEDs.

Experiment 2
Seedlings were grown under mixtures of red and blue LEDs in which 0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, or 100% of the photons were blue. (A mixture with 0% blue photons is red light only.)

Experiment 3
Seedlings were grown under a mixture of red and blue LEDs in which 25% of the photons were blue, at a photon flux of 100, 200, 300, or 400 µmol/m²/s.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Average dry mass and stem length of Species W seedlings after 21 days

prompt: In Experiment 1, what was the average dry mass of the seedlings grown under white LEDs?
explanation: The row labeled Exp. 1, white gives a dry mass of 200 mg. The value 180 mg is for red LEDs, 210 mg is for the 50% blue mixture, and 235 mg is the 25% blue mixture in Experiment 2.

passage_title: Mass of a Precipitate
passage:
When two solutions containing certain dissolved compounds are mixed, the compounds react to form a solid that does not dissolve, called a precipitate. Students studied a reaction between two unidentified colorless solutions, Solution X and Solution Y, that forms a white precipitate. In each trial, a volume of Solution X was added to 50.0 mL of Solution Y in a beaker, and the mixture was stirred for 10 minutes. The precipitate was separated by spinning the mixture in a centrifuge and pouring off the liquid; it was then rinsed, dried in an oven to constant mass, and weighed. The concentration of Solution X was 0.10 M (moles of dissolved compound per liter) in every trial. Unless stated otherwise, the concentration of Solution Y was 0.10 M, and both solutions were at 25 °C. Table 1 shows the results.

Experiment 1
Volumes of 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, and 120 mL of Solution X were added to Solution Y.

Experiment 2
A volume of 100 mL of Solution X was added to Solution Y having a concentration of 0.05 M, 0.10 M, 0.15 M, or 0.20 M.

Experiment 3
A volume of 60 mL of Solution X was added to Solution Y, with both solutions at 10 °C, 25 °C, 40 °C, or 55 °C. The mixture was kept at that temperature while it was stirred.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Mass of dried precipitate formed in each trial

prompt: In Experiment 1, what mass of precipitate formed when 60 mL of Solution X was added?
explanation: The row labeled Exp. 1, 60 mL of X gives 0.45 g. The value 0.30 g is for 40 mL, 0.60 g is for 80 mL, and 0.75 g is for 100 mL or 120 mL.

passage_title: Winter Fish Die-Offs in a Northern Lake
passage:
Lake Teral is a small lake, 8 m deep at its deepest point, in a cold northern region. It is covered by ice from early December to early April every year. In 4 of the past 12 winters, large numbers of dead fish were found along the shore when the ice melted (a winter die-off). Two fish species live in the lake. Species A cannot survive for more than a few days in water containing less than 3 mg/L of dissolved oxygen (DO); Species B can survive at DO as low as 1 mg/L. Both species are killed within days by dissolved ammonia concentrations above 2 mg/L. In all 4 die-off winters, snow more than 25 cm deep lay on the ice from January onward; in the other 8 winters, the snow on the ice was never more than 10 cm deep. Two scientists explain the die-offs.

Scientist 1
The ice seals the lake off from the air, so no oxygen can enter the water from the atmosphere. The only source of new oxygen under the ice is photosynthesis by algae, which requires light passing through the ice. Clear ice lets light through, but deep snow on the ice blocks almost all of it. Meanwhile, bacteria decomposing dead plant material on the lake bottom use up oxygen all winter. In snowy winters photosynthesis stops, and by February DO falls below 3 mg/L at every depth. Fish die from lack of oxygen, so whether a fish dies depends on how much oxygen its species requires.

Scientist 2
DO in the lake stays high enough for fish all winter, because algae just below the ice keep photosynthesizing with the small amount of light that passes through the snow. The die-offs are caused instead by ammonia, which bacteria release as they decompose dead plant material on the lake bottom. Ammonia builds up under the ice because it cannot escape to the air. Deep snow insulates the ice and keeps the bottom water slightly warmer, so decomposition is faster and more ammonia is released. In snowy winters, ammonia rises above 2 mg/L throughout the lake by late winter and kills fish of both species.

choices: the DO concentration falls below the level the fish need.
ammonia released by bacteria builds up under the ice.
the deep snow makes the water colder than the fish can tolerate.
algae under the ice release a toxin when they receive no light.
correct_answer: the DO concentration falls below the level the fish need.
explanation: Scientist 1 states that in snowy winters DO falls below 3 mg/L at every depth and that fish die from lack of oxygen. Ammonia buildup is the cause proposed by Scientist 2. Neither scientist says the water becomes too cold or that algae release a toxin.
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: identify a claim belonging to one viewpoint

passage_title: The Cool Dayside of Kessa b
passage:
Kessa b is a hypothetical gas giant planet that orbits very close to its star. It is tidally locked: one side (the dayside) always faces the star, and the other side (the nightside) never receives starlight. Infrared telescopes measured the average temperature of the dayside as 1,400 K and that of the nightside as 1,100 K. Astronomers calculated that if Kessa b absorbed all of the starlight striking it and all of that energy were radiated back into space from the dayside itself, the dayside temperature would be 1,900 K. The fraction of starlight that Kessa b reflects, and the location of the hottest point on its dayside, have not yet been measured. Two scientists explain why the dayside is cooler than 1,900 K.

Scientist 1
A layer of bright clouds made of tiny mineral droplets covers most of the dayside. The clouds reflect about 45% of the starlight back into space, so the dayside absorbs only about 55% of the starlight striking it. The atmosphere is calm, and very little heat moves from the dayside to the nightside, so the hottest point on the planet lies directly beneath the star (the substellar point). The nightside is warm because heat left over from the planet's formation is still escaping from its deep interior.

Scientist 2
Kessa b has no thick clouds on its dayside and reflects less than 5% of the starlight striking it. The dayside absorbs nearly all of the starlight, but winds blowing at several kilometers per second carry much of that heat around the planet to the nightside, where it is radiated into space. Because these winds blow from west to east, the hottest point is shifted about 30° east of the substellar point. Heat escaping from the planet's interior is too small to affect the temperature of either side.

the star gives off less light than was calculated.
correct_answer: winds carry much of the absorbed heat to the nightside.
